_doc: MACHINE-WRITTEN by `python deploy/make_invariants.py --bless <plugin> --wasm <path>`.
Do not hand-edit: every field here exists so the record cannot be typed wrong.
WHY A BLESSED HASH RATHER THAN A DERIVED ONE. Every other entry in the manifest is derived
from a file this repo tracks, so the repo IS the source of truth and drift means the box
disagrees with it. A plugin binary has no repo copy: the repo holds Rust, the box holds a
compiled .wasm, and there is no hash to derive. A manifest is a STATEMENT of what should be
deployed, so for a built artifact that statement has to be RECORDED at the moment someone
builds and deploys it. Blessing is that moment.
HOW A READER TELLS BLESSED-AND-CURRENT FROM A STALE PIN. Each record carries the sha256 of
the SOURCE that produced the binary: the plugin's own tracked files, plus wit/ and
crates/solana-core/, because those three determine the artifact. The generator recomputes
that hash every run. If the source has moved since blessing, the pin is stale and the
generator REFUSES to emit rather than baking a lie into the manifest. Emitting anyway needs
--allow-stale-binaries, and the manifest then records stale:true with the two hashes, so the
staleness is a fact on the box rather than a thing someone has to remember.
wit/ is in the source hash on purpose. The 2026-08-06 arity defect was one extra enum
variant in a vendored .wit file, and it made every plugin fail to instantiate while the
Rust was untouched. A source hash that ignored wit/ would have called those binaries
current.
A plugin with NO record here is not checked at all. That is honest rather than hidden: the
generator lists every such plugin under not_checked in the manifest and says so on stdout.
